paras: The killing of George Madden and the Winona lynching mob was an episode of mob violence at Winona, Shannon County, Missouri, in early March 1888, in which railroad laborers hunted Constable John Rucker after he was reported to have shot and killed the subcontractor George Madden. No report of Rucker's fate appears in the coverage, and a single Springfield dispatch said the laborers caught and lynched two of his friends and shot a third. Most papers carried the story as a St. Louis wire report of an "atrocious murder" followed by a "howling mob."

Madden held a subcontract on the Current River branch of the Gulf railroad, which was then being built through Winona. According to the Springfield dispatch, the village was full of unpaid day laborers, whom the contractors had calmed by blaming their own employers, McTigh & Co. of Memphis. The St. Louis wire said Madden, under pressure from his laborers, had repeatedly asked McKee, the superintendent of construction, for advance payments.

Accounts of the quarrel that followed differ. In the first St. Louis version, Madden threatened to shoot McKee on Saturday morning, March 3, and Rucker interfered; a second said Madden was drunk and refused a $150 advance. In the Springfield dispatch, unpaid laborers first hanged McKee until he was insensible, then revived him and let him go. Madden later fired at McKee on a train after being refused $1,500, and Rucker, trying to arrest him, was put off the train.

Every version agreed that Rucker then shot Madden dead from ambush; the Springfield dispatch said he sent nine rifle bullets into Madden on the Winona platform. Rucker went to a justice's office, was released on $1,000 bail within fifteen minutes and took to the woods, while the railroad hands "organized for a lynching." The Springfield dispatch said the laborers, "with whom Madden was a favorite," chased Rucker into the hills and that he killed several pursuers as he fled. Part of the mob, it said, returned to Winona, gathered more men and went after Rucker's friends, two of whom were caught and lynched while a third, barricaded in his house, was shot. None of these victims was named.

With no telegraph at Winona, the St. Louis wire said it was not known whether Rucker had escaped and that "the men have returned to work." The Springfield dispatch instead said fresh parties had vowed not to return until they had lynched Rucker. On March 9 the Washington Standard reported that "several lives were lost" in a conflict with the constable, and on March 15 an Iowa brief still did not know whether Rucker had escaped. No report of an inquest, arrests, a trial or Rucker's capture appears in the coverage.

The first St. Louis dispatch of March 5 ran the next day in the Indianapolis Journal, the Memphis Appeal and the St. Paul Daily Globe. Texas papers also printed it on March 6, with the Fort Worth Daily Gazette setting both St. Louis versions side by side, and the Emporia Weekly News and the Indian Chieftain carried it on March 8. Headlines cast Rucker as the criminal: "A Cowardly Murder" in the St. Paul Daily Globe, "A Brutal Murder at Winona, Mo." in the Memphis Appeal and "Pursued By a Howling Mob" in the Waco Daily Examiner. The wire called the shooting "uncalled for and cowardly" and described the pursuit, in some papers a "lynching bee," without comment.

Only the Sacramento Daily Record-Union printed the Springfield dispatch, under the headings "Sanguinary Affair" and "Bloody Deeds Done by Enraged Laborers in Missouri," making the laborers rather than Rucker the main actors. No paper named the race of anyone involved.

The reports conflict on how far the violence went. The St. Louis wire knew only of Madden's death, while the Springfield dispatch, sent a day later, added several pursuers killed, two friends lynched and a third shot. That account also placed the attack on McKee at "Van Buren, Ark.," a detail in no other report. Smaller differences concern the time of the shooting, given as Saturday morning in the St. Louis wire and Saturday night in a Winona brief.

reader.title: Killing of George Madden and the Winona lynching mob
bases: Railroad laborers organized to lynch Constable John Rucker after he killed George Madden and chased him into the woods (A1, A3); one dispatch says they caught and lynched two of his friends (A8).

A mob of laborers set out to lynch Rucker in revenge for Madden's killing (A1, A3, A8), and the Springfield dispatch alone says the mob caught and lynched two of Rucker's friends and shot a third (A8); the St. Louis wire knew only of Madden's death and said the men had gone back to work (A1), so the completed lynchings rest on one report, vaguely echoed by 'several lives were lost' (A11).

Several independent dispatches (St. Louis, Winona, Springfield) agree that Rucker shot Madden and fled a mob intent on lynching him (A1, A3, A7, A8); the lynching of Rucker's friends appears only in the Springfield dispatch (A8).

accounts.label: St. Louis wire (first version)
accounts.gist: Madden threatened to shoot McKee; Rucker interfered, then shot Madden from ambush, was bailed and fled pursued by a howling mob; fate unknown and the men returned to work.

accounts.label: St. Louis wire (second version)
accounts.gist: Madden, drunk, quarreled with McKee over a $150 advance; Rucker later shot him from ambush and fled a mob of laborers organized to lynch him; unknown if he was captured and killed.

accounts.label: Springfield dispatch
accounts.gist: Unpaid laborers hanged McKee until insensible; Madden fired at McKee on a train; Rucker killed Madden with a rifle at Winona, fled killing several pursuers, and the mob lynched two of his friends and shot a third.

accounts.label: Washington Standard brief
accounts.gist: A mob of railroad employes assaulted a contractor who refused pay and tried to lynch him; several lives were lost in a later conflict with the constable.

framing.detail: The St. Louis wire ran under headlines such as 'A Cowardly Murder', 'A Brutal Murder at Winona, Mo.' and 'Pursued By a Howling Mob', condemning Rucker's killing of Madden and reporting the 'lynching bee' without comment.
The Sacramento Daily Record-Union headed the Springfield dispatch 'Sanguinary Affair' and 'Bloody Deeds Done by Enraged Laborers in Missouri'.
